v.q: A payment API runs on three instances behind a load balancer. Customers are randomly logged out. What is the most likely cause?
o: The session is kept in each instance's own memory
The load balancer is using too many instances and needs fewer
The database transaction isolation level is set too low
The JWT signing algorithm is not strong enough
v.w: A session stored in one instance's memory is unknown to the others, so a request routed elsewhere looks logged out. Share the session (Redis) or use tokens.

v.q: Which design lets any instance serve any request?
o: Keep session state in a shared store
Keep the session in instance memory
Pin users to an instance
Store the session in a static field
v.w: Stateless instances can be added, removed and replaced because state lives outside them.

v.q: What is the main weakness of sticky sessions?
o: The session is lost when the pinned instance restarts or is replaced
They make the load balancer reject all new clients
They stop a service from using HTTPS between instances
They require every request to be signed with a JWT
v.w: Stickiness only hides local state: when the instance dies, is redeployed or scaled in, its sessions are gone, and load can also become uneven.

v.q: Which statement about sticky sessions is NOT true?
o: They remove all shared state
The session is lost if the instance dies
Load can become uneven
They complicate rolling updates
v.w: They only pin a user to one instance. The state is still lost when that instance goes away.

v.q: A mobile app times out on POST /payments and retries. How do you prevent a double charge?
o: Send the same idempotency key with every attempt and store the result per key
Disable retries in the client for all payment calls
Add a longer timeout and ignore any duplicate requests
Run the payment inside a read-only database transaction
v.w: The unique key identifies the intent, so a repeat returns the saved result instead of charging again. Turning retries off just loses payments.

v.q: Which header carries the client generated key that makes a payment retry safe?
o: Idempotency-Key
Content-Length
Accept-Language
ETag
v.w: The server stores the result under the key and returns it again when the same key arrives.

v.q: Why should a Kafka consumer record the id of each processed message in the same transaction as its effect?
o: Brokers deliver at least once, so duplicates must be detected and skipped
It makes Kafka deliver each message exactly one time
It lets the broker delete messages without acknowledgement
It removes the need for consumer groups
v.w: Redelivery is normal. A processed-id table with a unique constraint, committed with the effect, makes the consumer idempotent.

v.q: A consumer saves the message id and the business update in one transaction. What does it gain?
o: Duplicates are skipped safely
Exactly-once delivery by the broker
Faster publishing
No consumer groups needed
v.w: The broker may deliver twice. The stored id lets the consumer see that it already did the work.

v.q: Two users update the same account row at once. How does optimistic locking handle it?
o: The update with a stale version number fails and the caller retries
The database locks the row until the first user logs out
The second update silently overwrites the first one
Both updates are merged automatically by the database
v.w: UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? matches no row when someone else changed it first, so the second writer reloads and retries instead of overwriting.

v.q: Which statement about optimistic locking is NOT true?
o: It locks the row until the user logs out
It uses a version column
A stale update fails
The caller can reload and retry
v.w: Nothing is locked while the user thinks. The conflict is found at write time.

v.q: In event sourcing, how is the current account balance obtained?
o: By replaying the stored events, usually from the latest snapshot
By reading a balance column that every event overwrites
By asking the read model to recalculate it from scratch
By deleting old events and keeping only the last one
v.w: The events are the source of truth and are never edited. State is the fold of the events, and snapshots keep replay short.

v.q: In event sourcing, what is the source of truth?
o: The stored events
The read model
A cache
The latest snapshot only
v.w: State is derived from events. Snapshots and read models can be rebuilt from them.

v.q: What is the usual cost of using CQRS with separate read models?
o: The read side is eventually consistent, so it can lag behind a write
Writes can no longer be validated by business rules
Every query must lock the event store for reading
Read models cannot be rebuilt once they are created
v.w: Read models are updated after events are stored, so a screen may briefly show old data. They can be rebuilt from the events, and rules still apply on the write side.

v.q: Which claim about CQRS read models is NOT true?
o: The read side is always immediately consistent
A projection can lag behind a write
Read models can be rebuilt
Reads and writes can scale separately
v.w: The usual price is eventual consistency between the two sides.

v.q: Why does a database on Kubernetes normally use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
o: Pods keep a stable name and their own persistent volume across rescheduling
It makes the pods start faster than ordinary pods
It removes the need for any storage or backups
It lets all pods share one writable filesystem automatically
v.w: A StatefulSet gives db-0, db-1 and so on a stable identity and a volume each, so a rescheduled pod returns with the same data. Backups are still needed.

v.q: Which Kubernetes feature gives each database pod its own stable volume?
o: StatefulSet
Deployment
ReplicaSet
DaemonSet
v.w: A StatefulSet gives pods stable names and a persistent volume per pod.
